title: The long-distance champion of the skies
text: The wandering albatross is famous {{1}} its endurance: a bird {{2}} may not touch land during its first six years of life. It can glide for hundreds of kilometres {{3}} once flapping its wings. Biologists have long wondered {{4}} it manages such distances on so little food. The answer is that the albatross does not fly by flapping {{5}} by harvesting energy from differences in wind speed above the waves, a technique called dynamic soaring. Measured this way, an albatross spends {{6}} energy in flight than most songbirds spend hopping between branches. {{7}} a result, individuals have been tracked travelling over a hundred thousand kilometres in a single year. They return {{8}} solid ground only to breed, which for some birds happens once every two years.

gaps.hint: relative: a bird ___ may not touch land
gaps.explanation: Non-defining relative after the comma describing the bird.
'Without' + gerund expresses the action that never happens.
The manner is unknown: wondered how it manages.

gaps.hint: conjunction: not by flapping ___ by harvesting
gaps.explanation: 'Not … but …' — the second contrasting means takes 'but'.
Uncountable 'energy' and a comparative: spends less energy than.
'As a result' is the fixed linking phrase.
